questions.question: What is `origin`?
options: The default name Git gives to the remote you cloned from
The first commit in the repository
A reserved name that always points to GitHub
questions.explanation: A remote is a named URL of another copy of the repository. `origin` is just a convention; you can rename it or add more remotes, such as `upstream` for the project you forked.

questions.question: Which command shows the remotes of your repository together with their URLs?
questions.explanation: `-v` (verbose) lists each remote twice, with its fetch and push URL. `git remote show origin` gives more detail: tracked branches and whether they're up to date.

questions.question: You created an empty repository on GitHub and have a local repository with commits. Which command connects the two?
questions.explanation: `git remote add <name> <url>` stores the URL under a name. Then push with `git push -u origin main`. Cloning would create a second, separate local repository.

questions.question: What does `-u` do in this command?
options: It sets `origin/feature/login` as the upstream, so later a plain `git push` and `git pull` know where to go
It updates the branch even if the remote has newer commits
questions.explanation: `-u` is `--set-upstream`. You need it once per new branch. Since Git 2.37, `git config --global push.autoSetupRemote true` does this automatically on the first push.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
options: `fetch` only downloads new commits and updates `origin/*`; `pull` fetches and then merges (or rebases) into your current branch
`fetch` downloads one branch; `pull` downloads all branches
They do the same thing; `pull` is the older name
questions.explanation: `git fetch` is always safe: your own branches and files don't change. It lets you inspect first, for example with `git log main..origin/main`, and integrate after. `git pull` = `git fetch` + `git merge` (or `git rebase` with `--rebase`).

questions.question: What is `origin/main` in your local repository?
options: A read-only local copy of where `main` was on `origin` the last time you fetched
A live connection to the `main` branch on GitHub
Your local `main` branch after you push
A branch you can commit to that pushes automatically
questions.explanation: Remote-tracking branches only move when you `fetch`, `pull` or `push`. That's why `git status` can say "up to date with 'origin/main'" while GitHub has newer commits: run `git fetch` to refresh.

questions.question: `git push` fails with "rejected … (fetch first)": a colleague pushed to `main` before you. What do you do?
options: `git pull` (or `git pull --rebase`), fix any conflicts, then `git push`
Delete your local `main` and clone again
Wait a few minutes and push again
questions.explanation: Git refuses a push that would throw away commits on the remote. Integrate them first, then push. Forcing would delete your colleague's work from the shared branch.

questions.question: Why is `git push --force-with-lease` safer than `git push --force`?
options: It refuses to overwrite the remote branch if it has commits you haven't fetched
It asks for confirmation before pushing
It creates a backup branch on the remote
It only works on branches you created
questions.explanation: `--force` overwrites whatever is there. `--force-with-lease` checks that the remote still points where your `origin/<branch>` says. If someone pushed in the meantime, the push is rejected. A `git fetch` updates that expectation, so check what came in before retrying.

questions.question: Branches deleted on GitHub still show up in `git branch -r`. Which command cleans those up?
questions.explanation: `--prune` (`-p`) deletes remote-tracking branches whose branch no longer exists on the remote. Enable it permanently with `git config --global fetch.prune true`. Your own local branches are left alone.

questions.question: The repository moved to a new GitHub organisation (or you're switching from HTTPS to SSH). How do you point `origin` at the new URL?
questions.explanation: `set-url` changes an existing remote. `remote add` fails because `origin` already exists. The setting itself lives at `remote.origin.url` in `.git/config`.

questions.question: `git status` says: "Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits." What does that mean?
options: You have two local commits that aren't pushed yet
The remote has two commits you haven't pulled
Two files are modified but not committed
Your branch is two commits behind and must be rebased
questions.explanation: "Ahead" means you have commits the remote doesn't; `git push` sends them. "Behind" means the remote has commits you don't. "Have diverged" means both, so you have to pull (merge or rebase) before you can push.

questions.question: A colleague pushed a branch `bugfix/vat` and asks you to test it. You don't have it locally yet. What do you run?
questions.explanation: `git fetch` downloads the new branch as `origin/bugfix/vat`. When no local branch has that name, `git switch bugfix/vat` creates one that tracks the remote branch automatically. Switching to `origin/bugfix/vat` directly would put you in detached HEAD.

questions.question: You cloned your **fork** of an open-source project. How do you get the new commits from the original project into your local `main`?
options: `git remote add upstream <original url>`, `git fetch upstream`, then `git merge upstream/main`
`git clone <original url>` into the same folder
questions.explanation: Your fork is `origin`, and by convention the original project is `upstream`. Fetch from it, integrate it into your `main`, then `git push origin main` to update your fork on GitHub too. GitHub's "Sync fork" button does the server-side part.

questions.question: What does this command do?
options: Pushes your current commit to a branch called `review/vat-fix` on `origin`, whatever your local branch is called
questions.explanation: A push takes a **refspec** `<local>:<remote>`. Left of the colon is what you send, right is the branch name on the remote. With nothing on the left (`:review/vat-fix`) it deletes that remote branch.
